Machine learning usage in particle accelerators can be categorized into three levels of time granularity: nearreal-time,intermediate(∼1Hz)scale,anddelayedorofflineprocessing. Sometasks,suchasimagepro- cessing, segmentation, and classification can occur at a variety of time scales, depending on use case. These classifications are helpful to understand how the use of ML and AI in the particle accelerator community is different from that used in industry. Industry has generally focused on two major fields of research: image processing and language processing. At particle accelerators, while image processing is used in operations for some tasks such as sample alignment, most of these tasks occur outside the operational space. These tasksaremostoftenseenintheexperimental,medical,anddetectorportionsofmachines. Operationsneeds 10 includebeamlineandcontroloptimization, andrecentlyhaveseensignificantsuccessinusingBayesianopti- mization techniques. Recent work has addressed early detection of error states and alarms, both online and in post-processing. Operations data is also not generally treated with the same priority as experimental data, leading to sig- nificant differences in data granularity and archival terms. Previously, mainly figures of merit or summation metricssuchasbeampoweranddeviceperformanceonlongertimescaleswereallthatwasarchived,bothto minimize data storage needs and also due to a lack of consideration for the need for higher resolution data. The lack of high quality archival datasets leads to significant challenges for the training of smart systems, requiring either a significant amount of pre-processing of human readable machine log data, with its own errors, or interpolation and use of intensive manual labeling of datasets. This is one reason that optimization techniques have become the main focus of contemporary ML in operations. The other is that collaborations between facilities requires both desire for high quality data on a system with its own unique qualities and agreements in data usage between a number of disparate parties. Thesepartiesincludefundingentities(e.g. DOE),facilityoperations(subcontractors),divisionmanagement and staff, while also following any required privacy and data handling requirements levied by government and regional authorities. Several labs have become key, unofficial “centers” for machine learning in accelerator operations. These areprimarilySLACNationalAcceleratorLaboratory(SLAC)andJeffersonLaboratory(JLAB),withFermi National Accelerator Laboratory (FNAL) struggling to build up an AI/ML infrastructure for reasons given below. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) has been actively providing support for cutting edge technologies, and develops a significant portion of the simulation codes used in operations, but is much less actively involved aside from being the home center to funding for several key projects (i.e. the WarpX computing framework, and the SciDAC FastMATH Institute). The federal government has determined that AI and ML are key technologies for development in the USA, with the National Science Foundation (NSF) creating a pilot program called the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR). The NAIRR report of January 2023 recommends that significant investment be put towards AI/ML across the government, but with a more broad focus on non-critical (i.e. facility,operations,andinternal)usage[4].
